title: Evaluation of Tilt-correction of Anteversion on Anteroposterior Pelvic Radiographs in Total Hip Arthroplasty

sections.title: Why Cup Angle Measurement Matters
sections.markdown:
When a surgeon replaces a hip, one of the things that determines whether the new joint works well is how the artificial socket, the acetabular cup, is angled inside the pelvis. Get it wrong and the implant wears faster, loosens sooner, and the hip is more likely to dislocate. So checking that angle afterward matters. In practice, that check is almost always done with a plain X-ray taken from the front, an **anteroposterior (AP) pelvic radiograph**, because X-rays are cheap, available, and involve little radiation.

The problem is that an X-ray flattens a three-dimensional pelvis onto a two-dimensional image, and the answer you get depends on how the patient was lying or standing. The main culprit is **pelvic tilt**: how far the pelvis is rotated forward or backward relative to the vertical plane of the image. Tilt barely affects one of the two cup angles (inclination, the side-to-side tilt of the cup), but it badly distorts the other. **Anteversion**, how far the cup faces forward, is read off the shape of the ellipse the cup rim traces on the film, and that ellipse changes shape as soon as the pelvis rotates.

Researchers have proposed several ways to mathematically undo this distortion. This study tested the most widely cited one and asked a simple question: does it actually work on the kind of X-rays hospitals really take, in the kind of patients who really get hip replacements?

sections.title: The Tilt-Correction Method Being Tested
sections.markdown:
## The method being tested

The correction comes from work by Tannast and colleagues. They found that the vertical distance on an X-ray between the top of the pubic symphysis (the joint at the front of the pelvis) and the sacrococcygeal joint (where the tailbone meets the sacrum) tracks pelvic tilt closely. That measurement is called the **symphococcygeal distance (SCD)**. Measure it, look it up on a sex-specific nomogram (a printed lookup chart) alongside the raw anteversion reading, and the chart returns a tilt-corrected anteversion value.

Two things made the authors suspicious. Tannast's original X-rays were taken under tightly controlled conditions, with a fixed 1.2 m source-to-image distance, patients supine, and the beam aimed at a specific landmark. Routine post-operative films are not taken that way. And Tannast's patients averaged about 32 years old and were being treated for impingement or hip dysplasia, not hip replacement.

sections.title: Study Design and Navigation Reference Standard
sections.markdown:
## How they checked it

The team retrospectively reviewed patients who had a primary or revision hip replacement by one surgeon between February 2016 and February 2017, all done using the Intellijoint HIP navigation system. Standing AP X-rays taken two weeks after surgery were measured with templating software, scaled using the known diameter of the implanted femoral head. Every measurement was made three times and averaged, by a single researcher who did not know the navigation values.

The reference standard was the navigation system itself. During surgery, a camera is pinned to the patient's iliac crest and a tracker is attached to the femur or to surgical tools. Because the camera moves with the patient, the angle it reports is the cup's actual orientation in the body, unaffected by how the patient is positioned or imaged. That gives an independent ground truth to compare against.

Of 77 eligible cases, one was dropped for a pelvic fracture and five for X-rays too poor to measure, leaving 71 in the baseline group.

sections.title: Results: Limited Applicability and Systematic Overcorrection
sections.markdown:
## What they found

The correction method mostly could not be used at all. The sacrococcygeal joint simply was not visible on 44% of the X-rays (31 of 71). Among the 40 films where it was visible, another 9 produced values that fell off the edge of the nomogram's printed scale. In the end the correction worked on only 31 of the original 71 cases, 44%.

Where it did work, it made things worse rather than better:

- Corrected anteversion averaged 36.9° (SD 7.4°), versus 25.2° (SD 7.6°) uncorrected, a shift of 13.5° (p<0.001).
- Navigation, the ground truth, gave 27.4° (SD 5.7°) — much closer to the uncorrected reading than to the corrected one.
- Correlation between corrected values and navigation was essentially nil, r = -0.07. Corrected values tracked uncorrected values reasonably well (r = 0.73), meaning the correction was mostly just adding a roughly constant amount rather than responding to actual tilt.
- Raw uncorrected X-ray readings differed from navigation by an average of only -2.2° (SD 8.7°).

The measurements themselves were reliable, so the failure was not sloppy reading. Repeat measurements agreed almost perfectly, with intraclass correlations of 0.99 for both anteversion and SCD.

The direction of the error carries clinical weight. The correction inflated anteversion in every single case. A surgeon who trusts that inflated number would believe the cup is turned further forward than it is, and might aim for less anteversion next time, which raises the risk of posterior dislocation.

sections.title: Explaining the Failure and What It Means
sections.markdown:
## Why it failed here

The authors point to the gap between Tannast's laboratory-grade imaging protocol and everyday clinical radiography, the large age and diagnosis difference between the two patient groups, and an ambiguity in the original paper: Tannast never specified whether the vertical SCD was measured relative to a pelvic landmark or to the X-ray plane, nor how the images were scaled. Magnification on clinical films can vary from 97% to 127%, while templating software typically assumes a fixed 115% or 120%.

The conclusion is narrow and clear. On ordinary post-operative X-rays of hip replacement patients, the SCD correction cannot be applied most of the time, and when it can, it does not recover the true cup angle. Correcting for pelvic tilt on plain radiographs still needs a workable method.
